lessonTitle: A Structured Approach to Chest Pain, Breathlessness and Abdominal Pain

blocks.text: At 3 a.m. a 58-year-old taxi driver tells you he has 'indigestion' that started an hour ago, with a heavy feeling in the centre of his chest and a cold sweat. Whether you hear a stomach problem or a heart attack depends on the questions you ask next, and on the order in which you ask them.

blocks.markdown: Chest pain, breathlessness and abdominal pain account for a very large share of acute presentations. Each has a long list of possible causes, but clinicians do not memorise lists: they use a **structured approach**. They take a focused history to separate causes, build a **prioritised differential** (dangerous causes first, then common ones), and choose **initial investigations** that answer a specific question.

blocks.title: Prioritised differential diagnosis
blocks.text: A **differential diagnosis** is the set of conditions that could explain a presentation. It is **prioritised** by weighing (1) how likely each is given the patient's age, sex and risk factors and (2) how dangerous it would be to miss. Dangerous conditions that must be actively excluded are often called 'cannot-miss' diagnoses.

blocks.markdown:
### Chest pain: the focused history

Start with an open question, then characterise the pain with a framework such as **SOCRATES** (Site, Onset, Character, Radiation, Associated symptoms, Time course, Exacerbating/relieving factors, Severity). Then ask about risk factors (smoking, hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidaemia, family history of early heart disease, recent immobility or surgery) because they change the probability of each cause. Remember that your goal is not to label the pain but to distinguish **cardiac, vascular, pulmonary, gastro-oesophageal and musculoskeletal** causes.

blocks.caption: Discriminating features in chest pain
rows: Central pressure or tightness, may radiate to arm or jaw; exertional or at rest
Abrupt, severe, tearing pain maximal at onset, often radiating to the back
Hypertension; differing arm blood pressures; neurological symptoms
Pleuritic pain (sharp, worse on inspiration), often with breathlessness
Recent immobility or surgery; leg swelling; haemoptysis
Fever, purulent sputum, focal chest signs
Sharp central pain, worse lying flat and relieved by sitting forward
Burning retrosternal pain, related to meals or lying flat
Localised pain reproduced by palpation or movement

blocks.title: Using the history to discriminate
blocks.prompt: A 33-year-old man had a sore throat and fever last week. Today he has sharp central chest pain that is worse when he lies flat and better when he leans forward. He is not breathless. Which diagnosis fits best, and which cannot-miss diagnosis must still be considered?

steps.text: Characterise the pain: sharp, central, positional (worse supine, better sitting forward). Positional pain points away from ischaemic pressure pain and towards pericardial inflammation.
Note the context: a recent viral illness is a typical preceding event for viral pericarditis.
Check the alternatives: ischaemic pain is usually pressure-like and not positional; pleuritic pain is worse on breathing in; reflux is burning and meal-related.
Identify what must still be excluded: acute coronary syndrome and pulmonary embolism are cannot-miss even in a young patient, so obtain an ECG and a basic set of observations before settling.
Choose confirmatory tests: 12-lead ECG (diffuse changes may support pericarditis), chest X-ray, and bloods including troponin and inflammatory markers per local guidance.

blocks.answer: Acute pericarditis is the leading diagnosis, but an ECG and troponin are still needed to exclude myocardial ischaemia and other cannot-miss causes.

blocks.markdown:
### Breathlessness and abdominal pain: building the differential

For **breathlessness**, ask about speed of onset (seconds, hours, days, weeks), triggers (exertion, lying flat, allergens, cold), associated symptoms (wheeze, cough, sputum, chest pain, leg swelling) and past history. Think in systems: **airway** (asthma, COPD), **parenchyma** (pneumonia, interstitial disease), **pleura** (pneumothorax, effusion), **vascular** (pulmonary embolism, heart failure) and **other** (anaemia, metabolic acidosis, anxiety).

For **abdominal pain**, locate it by region (epigastric, right upper quadrant, periumbilical, right or left iliac fossa), note its character (colicky, constant, burning), and ask about vomiting, bowel habit, urinary symptoms, and in women of reproductive age the menstrual history and possibility of pregnancy.

blocks.caption: Region and common abdominal causes
rows: Myocardial ischaemia can present as epigastric pain; perforation
Ectopic pregnancy in women of reproductive age
Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm in older patients

blocks.title: Prioritising abdominal pain and choosing tests
blocks.prompt: A 24-year-old woman has 18 hours of right iliac fossa pain that began around the umbilicus and then moved. She is anorexic, has vomited once, and has a temperature of 37.9 degrees Celsius. Her last period was 6 weeks ago. Build a prioritised differential and choose initial tests.

steps.text: Interpret the pain pattern: periumbilical pain migrating to the right iliac fossa with anorexia and low-grade fever is typical of acute appendicitis, which is common and can be dangerous if perforation occurs.
List the other causes in this site: ovarian cyst complications or torsion, pelvic inflammatory disease, urinary tract infection, mesenteric adenitis.
Identify the cannot-miss diagnosis dictated by the history: a missed period means ectopic pregnancy must be excluded.

Choose tests that answer specific questions: urine pregnancy test (before imaging and surgery), urinalysis (urinary infection), full blood count and CRP (inflammatory response), and imaging (ultrasound, or CT in some patients) guided by the findings and local pathway.
Prioritise action: examine for peritonism, give analgesia, make nil by mouth if surgery is likely and request urgent senior surgical review.

blocks.answer: Appendicitis is the leading diagnosis; ectopic pregnancy must be excluded with a pregnancy test. Urinalysis, blood tests and imaging complete the initial work-up.

blocks.markdown:
### Choosing and justifying initial investigations

Every test should be linked to a question. Ask: *Which diagnosis will this test rule in or out, and will the result change what I do?* Initial investigations for common presentations typically include:

- **Chest pain:** a 12-lead ECG without delay for any suspected cardiac cause, high-sensitivity troponin (timed according to the local protocol, because a single early value may be normal), chest X-ray, and observations.
- **Breathlessness:** oxygen saturation and full observations, chest X-ray, ECG, blood tests including full blood count, and tests directed by suspicion (peak flow in suspected asthma, natriuretic peptide for suspected heart failure, blood gas if unwell).
- **Abdominal pain:** observations, bloods (full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver function tests, CRP, and amylase or lipase if pancreatitis is suspected), urinalysis, and pregnancy test where relevant, with imaging chosen by suspected cause.

items: Take the history from open to closed questions and always include onset, character, associated symptoms and risk factors.
Write down the leading diagnosis and the cannot-miss alternatives before ordering tests.
State what each test is for, and what you will do with the result.
Re-evaluate the differential as results return and as the patient's condition changes.

blocks.title: Justify the investigation
blocks.text: In OSCEs and on the ward, name the diagnosis a test addresses. 'ECG to look for ST elevation or other ischaemic changes' is far stronger than 'ECG because it is standard'.

points: A focused history, guided by SOCRATES and risk factors, discriminates cardiac, vascular, pulmonary, gastrointestinal and musculoskeletal causes of chest pain.
Prioritise the differential by likelihood and danger, using systems for breathlessness and regions for abdominal pain; always name the cannot-miss diagnoses.

Each initial investigation should be justified by the diagnosis it addresses and its effect on management, for example ECG for suspected cardiac pain or a pregnancy test for lower abdominal pain in a woman of reproductive age.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension describes sudden, severe pain that was maximal at onset and 'tearing' in character, radiating between his shoulder blades. Which diagnosis must be considered first?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: abrupt tearing pain maximal at onset and radiating to the back with hypertension is the classic pattern.
distractorRationale.b: Reflux is burning and related to meals or posture.
distractorRationale.c: Musculoskeletal pain is localised and reproducible on palpation.
distractorRationale.d: Pericarditis is positional and follows a different pattern.

questions.explanation: The abrupt onset, tearing quality, radiation to the back and hypertension are the discriminating features of aortic dissection. It is a cannot-miss diagnosis, so it must be actively considered even if other causes are more common.

questions.stem: Which history finding most strongly favours a musculoskeletal cause of chest pain?

options.text: Pain that is reproduced by pressing on the chest wall or moving the arm
Central pressure with sweating and nausea
Pain that began suddenly and is maximal at onset
Pain that follows a recent long-haul flight with unilateral calf swelling

questions.correctOptionText: Pain that is reproduced by pressing on the chest wall or moving the arm

distractorRationale.a: Correct: reproducibility on palpation or movement points to a local chest wall source.
distractorRationale.b: Pressure with autonomic features suggests myocardial ischaemia.
distractorRationale.c: Abrupt maximal pain raises concern for dissection or other vascular catastrophe.
distractorRationale.d: Recent immobility with unilateral leg swelling suggests venous thromboembolism.

questions.explanation: Reproducibility on palpation or movement is a helpful discriminator for chest wall pain, although it does not completely exclude serious causes. The other options each describe a feature that points to a cardiac or vascular cause.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old student has recurrent breathlessness with cough and wheeze, worse at night and after exercise. He has eczema, and there is no fever or chest pain. Which is the most likely diagnosis, and which initial bedside test best supports it?

options.text: Asthma; peak expiratory flow measurement, ideally showing variability

questions.correctOptionText: Asthma; peak expiratory flow measurement, ideally showing variability

distractorRationale.a: Correct: episodic wheeze with nocturnal and exercise triggers and atopy fits asthma, and variable airflow obstruction supports it.
distractorRationale.b: Pneumothorax typically presents with sudden unilateral pleuritic pain and breathlessness, not recurrent wheeze.
distractorRationale.c: Heart failure is unlikely at this age without cardiac history and would not explain atopic wheeze.
distractorRationale.d: Anaemia causes exertional breathlessness without wheeze, and an ECG does not address the question.

questions.explanation: Recurrent variable symptoms with nocturnal and exercise triggers and atopy are the typical pattern of asthma. Peak flow variability is a simple bedside measurement of variable airflow obstruction.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman has 30 minutes of central chest tightness with sweating. What is the most appropriate first investigation?

options.text: A CT scan of the abdomen

distractorRationale.a: Correct: an ECG is immediately needed in suspected ACS to detect ST elevation and other ischaemic changes.
distractorRationale.b: Abdominal imaging does not address a suspected cardiac cause.
distractorRationale.c: A pregnancy test is irrelevant in a 61-year-old.
distractorRationale.d: An abdominal film does not evaluate myocardial ischaemia.

questions.explanation: A 12-lead ECG is the first test in suspected acute coronary syndrome because ST-elevation myocardial infarction needs rapid identification and treatment. It is quick, non-invasive and directly addresses the leading cannot-miss diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman presents with left iliac fossa pain and vaginal spotting. She thinks her period is about a week late. Which investigation is the priority before imaging or analgesic decisions are finalised?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: it addresses ectopic pregnancy, a life-threatening cause in this scenario.
distractorRationale.b: Amylase is for suspected pancreatitis, which is not suggested here.
distractorRationale.c: Liver tests do not address the leading dangerous diagnosis.
distractorRationale.d: Peak flow is a respiratory test.

questions.explanation: Lower abdominal pain with a missed period and bleeding in a woman of reproductive age means ectopic pregnancy must be excluded first. A pregnancy test is quick, cheap and changes management immediately.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man drinks heavily and has 12 hours of severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, with repeated vomiting. He is tender in the epigastrium without peritonism. Which choice best pairs the leading diagnosis with a justified initial blood test?

options.text: Acute pancreatitis; serum amylase or lipase

questions.correctOptionText: Acute pancreatitis; serum amylase or lipase

distractorRationale.a: Correct: alcohol, epigastric pain radiating to the back and vomiting suggest pancreatitis and a raised pancreatic enzyme supports it.
distractorRationale.b: Appendicitis typically migrates to the right iliac fossa, and peak flow is irrelevant.
distractorRationale.c: PE does not explain this pain pattern and amylase does not diagnose PE.
distractorRationale.d: Renal colic is flank-to-groin pain, and troponin alone does not address it.

questions.explanation: Alcohol use, epigastric pain radiating to the back and vomiting are characteristic of acute pancreatitis, which is supported by a raised serum amylase or lipase. Troponin may still reasonably be requested because myocardial ischaemia can present with epigastric pain, so other tests complement it.

questions.stem: True or false: a single normal troponin taken very soon after the onset of chest pain always excludes myocardial infarction, so no further assessment is needed.
questions.explanation: Troponin takes time to rise after myocardial injury, so timing matters and repeat sampling according to local protocol is needed when a very early value is normal. The history, ECG and clinical risk assessment must also be interpreted together.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man presents with acute breathlessness that started over two hours. Outline a prioritised differential diagnosis, explaining which causes you would exclude first and why.
markingGuide: Uses a framework such as airway, lung parenchyma, pleura, vascular and other causes
Names cannot-miss causes such as pulmonary embolism, acute pulmonary oedema or heart failure, tension pneumothorax, acute coronary syndrome and severe asthma or COPD exacerbation
Names common causes such as pneumonia and COPD exacerbation
Explains prioritisation by combining danger and likelihood given age and risk factors
Mentions the speed of onset and associated features as discriminators
Links priority to the need for immediate investigation or treatment
questions.explanation: A prioritised differential combines danger with probability and uses the history to move causes up or down the list. Naming cannot-miss causes first ensures that life-threatening problems are excluded before common benign ones are assumed.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman has 24 hours of right upper abdominal pain, fever and has noticed yellow eyes. Give the leading diagnosis, justify three initial investigations, and say what each would add.
markingGuide: Leading diagnosis: biliary disease with infection, most notably ascending cholangitis, with cholecystitis and other biliary causes as alternatives
Observations and early assessment for sepsis
Blood tests: full blood count and CRP (inflammation), liver function tests (cholestatic pattern), urea and electrolytes and blood cultures where sepsis is suspected
Ultrasound of the biliary tree to look for gallstones and duct dilatation
Each test linked to the question it answers and to what it will change
Recognises the need for urgent senior and specialist input if unwell
questions.explanation: Pain, fever and jaundice together suggest infection in an obstructed biliary system, a condition that can deteriorate quickly. Tests are chosen to confirm the cholestatic pattern, show obstruction and detect sepsis.

questions.stem: Describe how you would take a focused history from a patient with chest pain, so that you can discriminate between cardiac, pleuritic, oesophageal and musculoskeletal causes.
markingGuide: Opens with an open question, then characterises the pain using a framework such as SOCRATES
Asks about site, radiation, onset and character of the pain
Asks about exertional or positional pattern and relief with rest, position or antacids
Asks about associated symptoms: sweating, nausea, breathlessness, cough, fever, burning or meal relation
Asks about risk factors such as smoking, hypertension, diabetes, family history, and recent immobility or surgery
Links features to the likely cause for each category named
questions.explanation: A focused history uses structure to draw out the features that distinguish causes, rather than reciting questions at random. Risk factors alter pre-test probability, so they matter as much as the pain characteristics.
